raw_segments.text: Twenty years ago, a poor curate, never mind his name at this moment, fell in love with
a rich man's daughter.
She fell in love with him and married him, against the advice of all her friends who
consequently disowned her immediately after the wedding.
Before two years passed, the rash pair were both dead and laid quietly side by side under
one slab.
I have seen their grave.
It formed part of the pavement of a huge churchyard surrounding the grim, soot-black old cathedral
of an overgrown manufacturing town in Shire.
They left a daughter, which, at its very birth, Charity received in her lap, cold as that
of the snowdrift I almost stuck fast in tonight.
Charity carried the friendless thing to the house of its rich maternal relations.
It was reared by an antin law, called, I Come to Names Now Mrs. Reed of Gateshead.
You start, did you hear a noise?
I dare say it is only a rat scrambling along the rafters of the adjoining schoolroom.
It was a barn before I had it repaired and altered, and barns are generally haunted by
rats.
To proceed.
Mrs. Reed kept the orphan ten years.
Whether it was happy or not with her, I cannot say, never having been told.
But at the end of that time, she transferred it to a place you know, being no other than
Lode School, where you so long resided yourself.
It seems her career there was very honorable.
From a pupil, she became a teacher, like yourself.
Really, it strikes me there are parallel points in her history and yours.
She left it to be a governess.
There, again, your fates were analogous.
She undertook the education of the ward of a certain Mr. Rochester.
